**Given:** $d,m\ge1$, the Hermitian matrices $\mathsf H_d$, the trace pairing, the family $F_1,\ldots,F_m$, and the synthesis map defined in the preceding definition.

[F1] [[def-nrqmx-finite-hermitian-frame-and-gram-pseudoinverse]]: $\mathsf H_d$ is a real vector space, $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$, and $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$.

[F2] [[lem-qsm-dt-finite-trace-pairing-cyclicity]]: $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$ for finite square matrices.

[F3] [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]: every finite Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]]: in a real or complex inner-product space, $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$.



1.1 For Hermitian $A,B$, $\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{Tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ by [F2]. The trace is additive and real-homogeneous, so the pairing is real-valued, symmetric, and real-bilinear. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Diagonalize $A\in\mathsf H_d$ by [F3] with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Then $\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)=\sum_j\lambda_j^2\ge0$, with equality exactly when all $\lambda_j=0$, hence exactly when $A=0$. This proves positive definiteness and the displayed square-root formula. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $c\in\mathbb R^m$, bilinearity gives $c^\mathsf T Gc=\operatorname{Tr}((Sc)^2)=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\ge0$. For $X\in\mathsf H_d$, the vector $v$ with coordinates $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aX)$ satisfies $\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=c^\mathsf Tv$ for every $c$, so it is $S^*X$. By [F2], $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)$; hence the matrix of $S^*S$ is precisely $G$. The equality $\langle c,Gc\rangle=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ implies $\ker G=\ker S$: $Sc=0$ gives $Gc=0$, while $Gc=0$ gives $\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=0$ and hence $Sc=0$ by step 2.1. By [F4], $|\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$; expanding $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ and applying this bound gives $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$. Thus the formula is a norm. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, algebra] ∎

proposed_proof:
**Given:** The compact set $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, the smooth
amplitude $a$ supported in $K$ with $k\cdot a(k)=0$, the fixed SI laboratory
chart, and the fields defined above.

[F1] Schwartz space consists of actual smooth functions $f$ for which every
polynomially weighted derivative $x^\alpha\partial^\beta f$ is bounded; this
is the definition of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$.
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]])

[F2] A potential pair obeys $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and
$B=\operatorname{curl}A$; its Coulomb condition is $\operatorname{div}A=0$.
([[def-em-gauge-transformation]])

[F3] The complex plane-wave encoding uses the componentwise real part of
$e\exp(i\theta)$; the real-part map is real-linear, $i^2=-1$, and
$\partial_z\exp z=\exp z$. The chain rule applies to the affine real phase
$k\cdot x-c|k|t$.
([[def-em-complex-plane-wave]],
[[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]],
[[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]],
[[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]])

[F4] The vacuum energy density is
$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|E|^2+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}|B|^2$, with
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])

[F5] Continuous real functions on closed nondegenerate rectangles are Riemann
integrable; the Riemann integral over a rectangle is the common lower and upper
Darboux value, and iterated integrals over product rectangles agree with the
multiple integral. A derivative integrates to its endpoint increment on a
closed interval, and the multidimensional integral obeys the absolute-value
estimate. ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]],
[[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]],
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]],
[[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]])

[F6] The fixed inertial laboratory chart uses the positively oriented
coordinates $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and time $t\in\mathbb R$; the electromagnetic
fields are real vector-valued maps on this region. In SI units, $c$ is the
vacuum speed, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[E]=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$,
$[A]=\mathrm{T\,m}$, and $[B]=\mathrm T$.
([[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F7] Divergence, curl, and partial derivatives have the stated component
formulas. For real $k$ and complex $a$, the cross-product identity
$k\times(k\times a)=k(k\cdot a)-|k|^2a$ follows by applying the real vector
triple-product lemma to the real and imaginary parts of $a$.
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[lem-cm-cross-product-triple-identity]])

[A1] The adopted smooth Maxwell branch is
$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$,
$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, and
$\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ for smooth fields and
continuous sources. This packet uses the source-free case $\rho=0$, $J=0$.
([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]])



1.1 Since $K$ is compact and excludes $0$, it has positive distance from the origin. Thus extending $a$ by zero across a neighborhood of $0$ gives a smooth compactly supported map on all of $\mathbb R^3$. For any compact time interval $J$, each function $f_t(k):=a(k)\exp(-ic|k|t)$ and each of its $t$-derivatives is smooth and supported in $K$; all its derivatives are uniformly bounded on $K\times J$. Every integral in the Definition is therefore an ordinary Riemann integral of a continuous compactly supported function. Differentiating in $x$ or $t$ under the integral is justified because the corresponding difference quotients converge uniformly on $K$ for each fixed $(x,t)$: the phase derivatives in $(x,t)$ are bounded because $k$ ranges over $K$ and $t$ lies in $J$, while the complex exponential has unit modulus. The one-variable mean-value estimate for the exponential is therefore uniform in $k$. The absolute-integral estimate in [F5] then bounds the difference between the integrals by the volume of a containing cube times the uniform error, which tends to zero. Iterating this argument for the resulting derivatives proves existence and continuity of every mixed space-time derivative. [given, F3, F5, F6, construct]

2.1 For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, differentiating in $x$ multiplies the integrand by $(ik)^\beta$. To control a factor $x_j$, integrate the $k_j$-derivative of the product of the compactly supported factor and $\exp(ik\cdot x)$ over a containing cube. The one-dimensional FTC in [F5] gives zero boundary terms because the factor vanishes near both endpoints; Riemann-Fubini in [F5] integrates that identity over the other two coordinates. Repeating this argument transfers every monomial $x^\alpha$ to derivatives in $k$, leaving an integral of $\partial_k^\alpha((ik)^\beta f_t(k))$ times a unit-modulus exponential, up to the fixed factor of modulus one produced by integration by parts. Its absolute value is uniformly bounded in $x$ and locally uniformly in $t$. The same argument applies after any $t$-derivative, since it only adds the smooth factor $(-ic|k|)^q$ on $K$. By [F1], $A_+$, $A$, $E$, and $B$ are therefore Schwartz in $x$ at each $t$, with the claimed local bounds. [step 1.1, F1, F5, algebra]

3.1 Expanding $\prod_{j=1}^3(1+|x_j|)^2$ gives finitely many absolute monomials, each controlled by a Schwartz seminorm in [F1]. Hence each Schwartz component $h$ is bounded by $C_h\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-2}$. Applying this bound to $E$ and $B$ shows that $|E|^2$ and $|B|^2$ are bounded by a constant times $\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-4}$. Each one-dimensional factor has finite integral $\int_{\mathbb R}(1+|s|)^{-4}ds=2/3$; by Riemann-Fubini in [F5], the product bound is integrable on the increasing cubes. Formula [F4] therefore gives a finite box-exhaustion energy $W(t)$. [step 2.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

3.2 Put $\gamma:=(2\pi)^{-3/2}$. Direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}A=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i(k\cdot a(k)) \exp(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t))\,d^3k=0$. The identity $\varphi=0$ and [F2] show that $(\varphi,A)$ represents exactly the displayed $(E,B)$ and is in Coulomb gauge. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, algebra]

3.3 Put $q(k,x,t):=\exp(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t))$ and $\gamma:=(2\pi)^{-3/2}$. By [F3] and real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$, $E=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i c|k|a(k)q\,d^3k$ and $B=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int i(k\times a(k))q\,d^3k$. Differentiating each integrand using [F3], [F7], and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{div}E=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int -c|k|(k\cdot a(k))q\,d^3k=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int -k\cdot(k\times a(k))q\,d^3k=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB =2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int[-c|k|k\times a(k)+c|k|k\times a(k)]q\,d^3k=0$, and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE =2\gamma\operatorname{Re}\int[-k\times(k\times a(k))-|k|^2a(k)]q\,d^3k=0$. The last equality uses the cross-product identity in [F7] and $k\cdot a(k)=0$. These are the source-free equations in [A1], proving that the integrated fields satisfy the adopted smooth Maxwell branch. [step 1.1, step 2.1, A1, F3, F7, algebra]

4.1 The exponent $k\cdot x-c|k|t$ is dimensionless. Since $d^3k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, the assigned $[a]=\mathrm{T\,m^4}$ gives $[A]=\mathrm{T\,m}$; then $E=-\partial_tA$ has units $\mathrm{T\,m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ has units $\mathrm T$. These agree with [F6]. [F6, algebra] ∎

proposed_proof:
**Given:** Reals $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$.

[F1] The real numbers form a complete ordered field, and each nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root; a positive radicand has a positive root. [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]] [[thm-of-square-roots]]

[F2] For real $t$, $e^{it}=\cos t+i\sin t$, $|e^{it}|=1$, and $e^{i\pi}=-1$; complex modulus is the square root of the sum of squares of real and imaginary parts. Hence $|\cos t|\le1$, using order preservation by squaring on nonnegative reals. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]

[F3] The complex exponential satisfies $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$ for complex $a,b$. [[def-complex-exponential]] [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]

[F4] The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
derivatives $\cos$ and $-\sin$, and $\sin 0=0$. Every real $t$ is a limit point of $\mathbb R$:
for $\varepsilon>0$, $t+\varepsilon/2$ is a distinct point within distance
$\varepsilon$. Thus both functions are continuous on $\mathbb R$.
[[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]] [[def-limit-point-r]] [[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]

[F5] If a real function is continuous on a closed nondegenerate interval and differentiable on its interior, its endpoint difference equals its derivative at some interior point times the interval length. [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]



1.1 Rationalizing the definition of $R$ gives $R(s)=\bigl((1-s/2)^2-(1-s)\bigr)/(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s}) =s^2/\bigl(4(1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s})\bigr)$. The denominator is positive because $s<1$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For real $a,b$, let $d:=a-b$. By [F3], $e^{ia}-e^{ib}=e^{ib}e^{id/2}(e^{id/2}-e^{-id/2})$; [F2] gives $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|=2|\sin(d/2)|$. If $d\ne0$, apply [F5] to $\sin$ on the interval with endpoints $0$ and $d/2$; [F2] gives $|\cos|\le1$, so [F4] yields $|\sin(d/2)|\le|d|/2$. The same inequality is immediate for $d=0$. Thus $|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Put $t:=\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$, so $0<t\le1$. Since $1-s\ge1-\delta^2$, the nonnegative roots obey $\sqrt{1-s}\ge t$: otherwise the difference of their squares, factored as a product of a positive sum and positive difference, would give $1-s<1-\delta^2$. Hence $1-s/2+\sqrt{1-s}\ge1-\delta^2/2+t=(1+t)^2/2\ge2t^3$; the last inequality follows from $(1+t)^2\ge4t$ and $t\ge t^3$. Substitution into step 1.1 proves $0\le R(s)\le s^2/(8t^3)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $a:=zk_0\sqrt{1-s}$ and $b:=zk_0(1-s/2)$ in step 1.2. Then $|a-b|=|z|k_0R(s)$, so step 2.1 gives the stated multiplier bound. [given, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, scalar data $u_0$ supported

mode at $|\mathbf q|\le\delta k_0$.

$e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}$ on the support disk; the

[F2] Under countable choice, $\mathcal F_2$ is unitary on complex $L^2$ and
preserves its norm. [[thm-plancherel]] [[def-countable-choice]]

$|z|k_0s^2/[8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}]$. [[lem-emx-paraxial-phase-multiplier-bound]]

$E(\mathbf x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf e e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)})$;
the exponential is differentiable and its phase derivative follows the chain
rule. [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]

include $\operatorname{div}E=0$. [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]

$e^{-i\pi/2}=-i$. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]

[F6] Complex modulus is the Euclidean modulus of real and imaginary parts, and
the real transverse Euclidean norm is induced by the dot product; extend a real
dot product bilinearly when its second argument is complex. Order of squares
reflects order for nonnegative real numbers. [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]

aperture data or for exact vector Maxwell errors.

laboratory origin and orientation, and the SI vacuum constants.

$\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}A=0$, and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$.

$g=\varepsilon_0E\times B$ and $\ell=x\times g$, relative to the fixed
laboratory origin. ([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]])

[F3] $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$,
$[\varepsilon_0]=\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, $[E]=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and
$[A]=\mathrm{T\,m}=\mathrm{V\,s\,m^{-1}}$.
([[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F4] A continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle has a Riemann
integral; the all-space integrals here are limits over cubes, and iterated
integrals of a Riemann-integrable function on a product rectangle equal its
multiple integral. ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]],
[[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]],
[[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]])

Products of two such components, with at most one coordinate factor, are bounded by a constant times $\prod_j(1+|x_j|)^{-7}$, whose one-dimensional factors are integrable. For each canonical term, $\varepsilon_0EA$ has units $\varepsilon_0E^2\,\mathrm{s}$ because $A$ has the units of $E$ times time by [F3]. **Given:** $k\ne0$, the Euclidean orientation and cross product on $\mathbb R^3$,
their complex componentwise extensions, and the transverse Fourier amplitudes of
the classical field item above.

[F1] The amplitude space consists of smooth compactly supported maps
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$k\cdot a(k)=0$; the support avoids $0$.
([[def-emx-transverse-fourier-field]])

[F2] The cross product is the right-handed Euclidean cross product, is
bilinear, obeys $n\times(n\times v)=n(n\cdot v)-v$ for real $n$ and complex
$v$, and satisfies $(u\times v)\cdot w=\det[u,v,w]$, by its coordinate
formula. For real vectors its coordinate formula also gives
$|u\times v|^2=|u|^2|v|^2-(u\cdot v)^2$.
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]])

[F3] The real Euclidean dot product is $n\cdot v=\sum_jn_jv_j$; complex
conjugation and the Hermitian product are componentwise, with $i^2=-1$.
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
[[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]])

[A1] $R$ is a real matrix with $R^TR=I$ and $\det R=1$; these conditions
define the proper rotation group used here.



1.1 Since $n\cdot n=1$, the formula $P_Tv=v-n(n\cdot v)$ gives $n\cdot P_Tv=0$ and $P_Tv=v$ whenever $v\in T_k$; hence $P_T$ is idempotent with range $T_k$. Also $n\times n=0$, so $Cn=0$. Write $N_n v:=n\times v$. Its real matrix is skew-symmetric, so $N_n^T=-N_n$; with the Hermitian product of [F3], $(iN_n)^*=(-i)N_n^T=iN_n$, hence $C(k)$ is Hermitian. The vector triple product in [F2] gives $C(k)^2v=-n\times(n\times v)=v-n(n\cdot v)=P_T(k)v$. Also $P_T(k)^*=P_T(k)$ because $n$ is real, $P_T(k)^2=P_T(k)$, its range is $T_k$, and $C(k)n=0$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The cross product with $n$ is perpendicular to $n$, so $P_TC=C$; also $C(n(n\cdot v))=0$, so $CP_T=C$. Thus $P_TC=CP_T=C$. Since $C^2=P_T$, direct multiplication gives $$P_\sigma^2=\tfrac14(P_T+2\sigma C+C^2)=\tfrac12(P_T+\sigma C)=P_\sigma,\quad P_{+1}P_{-1}=\tfrac14(P_T-C^2)=0,\quad P_{+1}+P_{-1}=P_T.$$ Both are Hermitian by step 1.1. To verify their ranks, let $e_1,e_2$ be the first two coordinate unit vectors. They are linearly independent, so at least one, say $e_j$, is not parallel to $n$. Set $u:=(e_j-(e_j\cdot n)n)/|e_j-(e_j\cdot n)n|$; its denominator is positive, and $u$ is a real unit vector perpendicular to $n$. Put $v:=n\times u$. The norm identity in [F2] gives $|v|=1$, and the determinant identity gives $u\cdot v=0$; the triple-product identity gives $n\times v=-u$. Thus $u,v$ span the real transverse plane. For $w_+:=(u+iv)/\sqrt2$ and $w_-:=(u-iv)/\sqrt2$, expansion gives $\langle w_+,w_+\rangle_H=\langle w_-,w_-\rangle_H =\tfrac12(|u|^2+|v|^2)=1$ and $\langle w_+,w_-\rangle_H=\tfrac12(|u|^2-|v|^2-2i(u\cdot v))=0$. Hence $w_+,w_-$ span $T_k$, and the complementary orthogonal projectors $P_{+1},P_{-1}$ each have rank one there. The finite coordinate choice is only for this fixed $k$; no family of choices is made. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 The coefficients of $P_T(k)$ and $C(k)$ are smooth functions of $k\ne0$ because $n=k/|k|$ is smooth there. Step 2.1 shows that $P_\sigma(k)$ has range in $T_k$, so multiplication by it sends a smooth transverse amplitude supported in a compact set away from zero to another such amplitude. Since $U_t$ multiplies by the scalar $e^{-ic|k|t}$, $P_\sigma(k)e^{-ic|k|t}a(k)=e^{-ic|k|t}P_\sigma(k)a(k)$ pointwise, proving $M_\sigma U_t=U_tM_\sigma$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $R$ as in [A1], the map $R_*a$ is smooth and its support is the rotated compact set $R(K)$, which still avoids zero. Moreover $k\cdot R a(R^Tk)=(R^Tk)\cdot a(R^Tk)=0$ by $R^TR=I$, so $R_*a$ belongs to the amplitude class. Preservation of orientation gives $R(n\times z)=(Rn)\times(Rz)$: for every real $w$, $(Rn\times Rz)\cdot Rw=\det[Rn,Rz,Rw]=\det(R)\det[n,z,w] =(n\times z)\cdot w=(R(n\times z))\cdot Rw$, and nondegeneracy of the Euclidean inner product identifies the two vectors. Orthogonality gives $|Rk|=|k|$. Therefore $P_T(Rk)=RP_T(k)R^T$ and $C(Rk)=RC(k)R^T$, hence $P_\sigma(Rk)=RP_\sigma(k)R^T$. Substituting this identity into the definitions of $M_\sigma$ and $R_*$ gives $M_\sigma R_*a(k)=P_\sigma(k)Ra(R^Tk)=R P_\sigma(R^Tk)a(R^Tk) =R_*M_\sigma a(k)$. This proves the proper-rotation commutation claim; the determinant condition is what preserves, rather than reverses, the helicity label. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The standard basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ of $\mathbb C^2$, the associated projections $P_a=|a\rangle\langle a|$, and $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ consists of smooth functions whose polynomially weighted derivatives are bounded ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]).

[F2] The Weyl kernel and Wigner formula, the inner product convention, and the scaled Fourier transform are exactly those of [[def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner]].

[F3] The negative-sign Fourier transform preserves Schwartz space ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]).

[F4] Fourier inversion holds pointwise for Schwartz functions, with absolutely convergent inverse integral ([[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]]).

[F5] Absolutely integrable functions on a sigma-finite product may be integrated in either order ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F6] The normalized Gaussian Fourier integral is $\int e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}\,dy=2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-\xi^2/\epsilon}$ in dimension one ([[lem-euclidean-gaussian-fourier-transform-with-two-pi-normalization]]).

[F7] Integration by parts on the real line is valid for integrable derivative products with vanishing endpoint products ([[lem-complex-integration-by-parts-on-intervals-and-decaying-lines]]).


**Given:** The data of the Statement and [A1]–[F7].

1.1 The map $(x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,x-y)$ is an invertible linear map with absolute determinant $1$. The product of $a$, $u$, and $\overline u$ in the Weyl pairing is Schwartz in the transformed variables, so it is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5] and this change of variables give $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)u(q-r/2)\overline{u(q+r/2)}\,dq\,dr\,d\xi . $$ Substituting $y=-r$ turns the last two factors and the exponential into the defining integrand of $W_\epsilon[u]$; hence the pairing identity follows. [given, A1, F2, F5, algebra]

1.2 The function $g(x,y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz on $\mathbb R^{2d}$, because $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y/2,x-y/2)$ is invertible linear and products of Schwartz functions are Schwartz. Its full negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform $\widehat g(\eta,\zeta)$ is Schwartz by [F3]; applying inverse Fourier transformation in $\eta$ by [F4] gives the partial transform $\int e^{-2\pi i y\cdot\zeta}g(x,y)\,dy$, Schwartz jointly in $(x,\zeta)$. The desired partial transform with phase $e^{-iy\cdot\zeta'}$ is this function at $\zeta=\zeta'/(2\pi)$; frequency dilation preserves Schwartz space. Replacing $\zeta'$ by $\xi/\epsilon$ and multiplying by $(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}$ therefore gives $W_\epsilon[u]\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})\subset L^1$. Conjugating the defining integral and substituting $y\mapsto-y$ returns the same integral, so $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Fix $x$ and set $f_x(y):=u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}$. In the position marginal set $\eta=\xi/\epsilon$, so $d\xi=\epsilon^d d\eta$; write $\widehat f_x(\eta)=\int e^{-iy\cdot\eta}f_x(y)\,dy$, the rescaled negative-sign $2\pi$ transform. Then $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi)^{-d}\int\widehat{f_x}(\eta)\,d\eta=f_x(0)=|u(x)|^2, $$ where the middle equality follows from [F4] at zero after the change from the library frequency $\eta/(2\pi)$ to $\eta$. All integrals are absolutely convergent because $f_x,\widehat{f_x}\in\mathcal S$. [given, A1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.4 For the momentum marginal, $u\in\mathcal S\subseteq L^1$, so the double integral in $x,y$ is absolutely integrable by Fubini [F5]. The change $q=x+y/2,\ r=x-y/2$ has absolute determinant $1$ and $q-r=y$. Therefore $$ \int W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{-i(q-r)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(q)\overline{u(r)}\,dq\,dr=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$ The last equality is the product of the scaled Fourier integral with its complex conjugate. [given, A1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 To see that nonnegativity fails, set $v_\epsilon(x)=\sqrt{2/\epsilon}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/4}x e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. Substituting $x=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$ and applying [F6] at Gaussian parameter $1/4$ gives $\int e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi$; one integration by parts [F7] then gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\sqrt\pi/2$, hence $\int x^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon}dx=\sqrt\pi\,\epsilon^{3/2}/2$ and $\|v_\epsilon\|_2=1$. At the origin, $$ W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon](0,0)=-(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}\frac{1}{2\epsilon\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}}\int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}\,dy=-\frac1{\pi\epsilon}<0. $$ Here the Gaussian second moment is obtained from [F6] at $\xi=0$ by one integration by parts [F7]. Thus $W_\epsilon[v_\epsilon]$ is a normalized Schwartz Wigner distribution with a negative value. [given, A1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

**Given:** AC; a nonzero complex Hilbert space; a densely defined nonnegative self-adjoint $A$; $M>0$; and $J\in H$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[A2] [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]]: AC implies countable choice.

[F1] [[thm-qftx-positive-unbounded-spectral-calculus]]: for nonnegative self-adjoint $A$, the spectral measure is supported on $[0,\infty)$ and bounded Borel functions define bounded operators with norm at most their supremum.

[F2] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.

[F3] [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]: under countable choice the adjoint of a densely defined operator is closed; hence a self-adjoint $A$ is closed.

[F4] [[lem-qftx-finite-heavy-gaussian-square]]: the normalized finite Gaussian source-shift ratio is $\exp(\tfrac12j^TK^{-1}j)$ for symmetric positive-definite $K$.

[A3] [[def-hilbert-space]]: a complex Hilbert space is a complete complex inner-product space.

[A4] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the complex inner product is linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second.

[F5] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ as the inverse of $\exp$.

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 The actual proof of [F1] uses Cauchy–Schwarz for its resolvent lower bound and closedness of $A$ for its resolvent graph argument. [F2] supplies the former. By [A1]–[A2] countable choice is available, so [F3] applies and self-adjointness gives $A=A^*$, hence $A$ is closed. This records the actual inputs of [F1]'s proof; the carrier's complete conditional proof was inspected. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3]

[F4, F5, given, algebra] ∎

[F1] A smooth singular chain is a finite real linear combination of smooth
singular simplices. [[def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes]]

[F2] The integral over a smooth three-simplex is the Jordan Riemann integral

$T_3=\{z\in\mathbb R^3:z_i\ge0,\ z_1+z_2+z_3\le1\}$.
[[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]

[F3] Integration over a bounded Jordan set is defined by extending the
integrand by zero to a bounded containing rectangle and integrating there.
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]

[F4] On a rectangle, the Darboux integral is the common value of the
supremum of lower grid sums and infimum of upper grid sums; common refinements
preserve the integral criterion. [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]

[F5] A rectangle has finite volume, and cutting one coordinate interval
preserves total volume. [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]

[F6] A closed bounded subset of Euclidean space is compact.
[[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F7] A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly
continuous. [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]

[F8] For a continuously differentiable function on a closed interval, the
integral of its derivative is the endpoint increment.

The Darboux definitions [F4] give linearity: for integrable $u,w$, choose grid partitions whose upper-minus lower sums for each are arbitrarily small, take a common refinement, and use $\inf(u+w)\ge\inf u+\inf w$ and $\sup(u+w)\le\sup u+\sup w$ on each cell. The upper-minus-lower gap for $u+w$ is therefore bounded by the sum of the chosen gaps, so $u+w$ is integrable. Its lower and upper integrals are squeezed between the sums of the lower integrals of $u,w$ and the sums of their upper integrals; letting the gaps tend to zero gives $\int_Q(u+w)=\int_Qu+\int_Qw$. For a scalar $c>0$, upper and lower sums scale by $c$; for $c<0$ they exchange after scaling, giving $\int_Q(cu)=c\int_Qu$, and $c=0$ gives zero. [F4] A continuous positive-definite symmetric matrix family on a compact parameter set has uniform bounds $aI\le A^0\le bI$ for some $0<a\le b<\infty$ ([[lem-gr-positive-definite-symmetric-matrix-bounds]]).

[F2] [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]]: along each smooth path segment, transport is the unique solution of $U'=-\omega(\dot\gamma)U$, with later transport multiplying on the left.

[F3] [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]: $F=d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega$ is the curvature matrix two-form, and a Lorentz connection satisfies $\omega^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta\omega=0$.

[F4] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: solutions of a smooth parameter-dependent finite-dimensional ODE depend smoothly on the parameter on a common compact interval.

[F5] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: for a continuous matrix coefficient and arbitrary initial matrix, the linear matrix ODE has a unique solution on the given compact interval.

[F6] [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]: the fundamental group consists of based loops modulo endpoint-fixed path homotopy.

[F7] [[thm-qftx-cw-fundamental-group-presentation]]: a finite connected CW complex has the presentation with non-tree 1-cells as generators and 2-cell attaching loops as relators.

[F8] [[def-group-presentation]]: a presentation $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ is the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the normal closure of $R$.

[F9] [[prop-normal-closure-is-products-of-conjugates]]: the normal closure of a set is the set of finite products of conjugates of its elements and their inverses.

**Given:** The open star-shaped set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, its centre $a$,
the closed smooth $k$-form $\alpha$, and $1\le k\le n$.

[A1] $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is open and star-shaped about $a$, and $\alpha$
is a smooth closed $k$-form with $1\le k\le n$.

[F1] Star-shapedness means $a+t(x-a)\in U$ for every $x\in U$ and
$0\le t\le1$. [[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]

[F2] For a smooth map $F$, the pullback is
$(F^*\alpha)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)
=\alpha_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k)$.
[[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]]

[F3] The exterior derivative commutes with pullback:
$d(F^*\alpha)=F^*(d\alpha)$. [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-commutes-with-pullback]]

[F4] A continuous parameter derivative on a compact rectangle may be passed
through a Riemann integral. [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]

[F5] For a continuous function on a closed interval with an integrable
interior derivative, the integral of that derivative is the endpoint
increment. [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]



**Given:** As in [A1] and [F1]–[F5].

1.1 Define $F:[0,1]\times U\to U$ by $F(t,x)=a+t(x-a)$. By [F1] this map has image in $U$. In coordinates on $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, decompose its pullback as $F^*\alpha=\gamma_t+dt\wedge\eta_t$, where $\gamma_t$ is a $k$-form and $\eta_t$ a $(k-1)$-form on $U$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.2 Since $d\alpha=0$, [F3] gives $d(F^*\alpha)=0$. In product coordinates $d=d_U+dt\wedge\partial_t$, so the coefficient of $dt$ in this equality is $\partial_t\gamma_t-d_U\eta_t=0$. The pullback formula [F2] gives $(\eta_t)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}) =t^{k-1}\alpha_{a+t(x-a)}(x-a,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})$. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 The integrand defining $K\alpha$ is alternating and multilinear in $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$, so its integral is a $(k-1)$-covariant alternating tensor at each $x$. Its coefficient functions are smooth in $(x,t)$. Restricting $x$ to a compact coordinate rectangle inside $U$ and using [F4] on each coordinate derivative shows that parameter derivatives pass through the $t$-integral; iteration gives smooth coefficients, hence a smooth $(k-1)$-form $K\alpha$. [step 1.1, F4]

3.1 Thus $K\alpha=\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. By step 2.1 and [F4], $d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt=\int_0^1d_U\eta_t\,dt$. Apply [F5] to the coefficient functions of $\gamma_t$ and use step 1.2: $\gamma_1-\gamma_0=\int_0^1\partial_t\gamma_t\,dt =d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. Here $\gamma_1=\alpha$ because $F(1,x)=x$, while $\gamma_0=0$ because $F(0,x)=a$ is constant and $k\ge1$. Hence $d(K\alpha)=\alpha$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, F4, F5] ∎



The conclusion is local: each star-shaped coordinate domain is contractible.
It supplies local primitives only and gives no global cohomological
conclusion.

**Given:** AC, finite $d\ge1$, symmetric positive-semidefinite $C$, and the functions in the Definition.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: the finite-dimensional Gaussian-law definition assumes AC.

[F1] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: for positive-semidefinite $C$, the Borel probability $\gamma_C=N_d(0,C)$ exists, including singular $C$.

[F2] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for product-measurable nonnegative functions, parameter integrals are measurable and iterated integrals agree.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]]: $\log$ is defined on $(0,\infty)$ as the inverse of $\exp$.

[F4] [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $\exp$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.



**Proof technique:** direct measurability and positivity check.

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Definition.

1.1 The map $(x,z)\mapsto f(x+z)$ is Borel because addition is continuous and $f$ is Borel. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is sigma-finite because $\mathbb R^d=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[-n,n]^d$ and each cube has finite measure; $\gamma_C$ is a probability by [F1]. Thus [F2] makes $x\mapsto T_Cf(x)$ Borel, including when the integral is infinite. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 For finite nonnegative Borel $V$, $g_x(z):=e^{-V(x+z)}$ is Borel and satisfies $0<g_x(z)\le1$. Its integral against the probability $\gamma_C$ is at most one. It is strictly positive: if the integral were zero, each set $\{z:g_x(z)\ge1/n\}$ would have measure zero, while their countable union is all of $\mathbb R^d$, contradicting $\gamma_C(\mathbb R^d)=1$. Thus $T_C(e^{-V})(x)\in(0,1]$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3], the logarithm is defined at these values. Its continuity follows directly from [F4]: for $y_0>0$ and $\epsilon>0$, strict increase and continuity of $\exp$ give $\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon)<y_0<\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)$; put $\delta=\min\{y_0-\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon),\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)-y_0\}>0$. If $y>0$ and $|y-y_0|<\delta$, then $\exp(\log y_0-\epsilon)<y<\exp(\log y_0+\epsilon)$, and strict monotonicity gives $|\log y-\log y_0|<\epsilon$. Hence $V_C$ is finite, nonnegative, and Borel. If $C=0$, then for each coordinate $Z_i$, $\mathbb E Z_i^2=C_{ii}=0$. For every $n\ge1$, $0=\mathbb E Z_i^2\ge n^{-2}\mathbb P(|Z_i|\ge n^{-1})$, so $Z_i=0$ almost surely; the finite intersection gives $Z=0$ almost surely and $\gamma_0=\delta_0$; hence $T_0f=f$ and $V_0=V$. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $\epsilon,c,\lambda>0$, a period $L>0$, and the smooth real initial data and Cauchy problem in the Statement.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]): every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[def-csm-frontier-two-velocity-scaling]]: $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$, $dm_L=dx/L$, $\kappa_n=2\pi n/L$, and the two equations have transport speeds $\pm c/\epsilon$ and switching rate $\lambda/\epsilon^2$ in each direction.

[F2] [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the characters $y\mapsto e^{2\pi iny}$ form an orthonormal basis of complex $L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,dy)$ and Parseval's identity holds. The change of variable $y=x/L$ preserves normalized measure and carries these characters to $e_n(x)$, so the same coefficient expansion and Parseval identity hold on $\mathbb T_L$ with $dm_L$.

[F3] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: for a differentiable function $G$ on a closed interval with integrable derivative, $\int_a^b G'(x)\,dx=G(b)-G(a)$. For periodic $C^1$ functions on $[0,L]$, the right side is zero.

[F4] [[lem-linear-matrix-odes-have-unique-global-solutions-on-a-given-interval]]: for every compact interval $I$, continuous real matrix field $C$ on $I$, and initial time $t_0\in I$, the real linear matrix IVP $Y'=C(t)Y$ has a unique solution on all of $I$.

[F5] [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]: on a real or complex Banach space, a bounded operator $A$ has an operator-norm convergent exponential series $E(t)=\sum_{m\ge0}t^mA^m/m!$; $E'(t)=AE(t)$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\|\le\tfrac12t^2\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$.

[F6] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]]: for every integer $n\ge1$, $\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric is complete; in particular $\mathbb R^4$ with the Euclidean norm is a Banach space.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: on $\mathbb R^4$, $|x\cdot y|\le\|x\|_2\|y\|_2$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm.

[F8] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: on $\mathbb R^4$, $x\cdot y=\sum_{j=1}^4x_jy_j$ and $\|x\|_2=(x\cdot x)^{1/2}$.

[F9] [[def-operator-norm]]: for a bounded linear map $A$ on a normed space, $\|A\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Ax\|$ and $\|Ax\|\le\|A\|\|x\|$.



**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and the initial data of the Statement.

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $n\in\mathbb Z$, put $U_n=(\widehat f_+^\epsilon(n),\widehat f_-^\epsilon(n))^{\mathsf T}$, $v=c/\epsilon$, and $\alpha=\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Integrating by parts in the real and imaginary parts separately, using [F3], gives $U_n'=M_nU_n$, with $M_n=\begin{pmatrix}-i\kappa_n v-\alpha&\alpha\\ \alpha&i\kappa_n v-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$. Realify $z\in\mathbb C^2$ by $\mathcal Rz=(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_2)\in\mathbb R^4$, and for $M=P+iQ$ put $\mathcal RM=\begin{pmatrix}P&-Q\\Q&P\end{pmatrix}$. Direct coordinate multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Mz)=(\mathcal RM)\mathcal Rz$ and $|\mathcal Rz|_2^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$. By [F6], $\mathbb R^4$ is Banach; [F7] applied rowwise bounds $\mathcal RM_n$ as an operator, and [F8]–[F9] specify the Euclidean and operator norms. Hence [F5] makes $t\mapsto e^{t\mathcal RM_n}\mathcal RU_n(0)$ a solution of the realified constant-matrix IVP; [F4] gives uniqueness on each compact interval $[0,T]$, so these compatible solutions define the unique global complex Fourier mode solution after pulling back by $\mathcal R$. **Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the scaling and Fourier conventions of [[def-csm-frontier-two-velocity-scaling]], $c,\lambda,L>0$, and $\rho_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T_L)$ with $\rho_0\ge0$.

[F2] [[lem-csm-frontier-two-velocity-contraction]]: for these data the unique global smooth solution exists, and the two-component evolution contracts the $L^2(dm_L;\mathbb C^2)$ norm.

[F3] [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the characters $e^{2\pi iny}$ form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,dy)$, so Fourier expansions and Parseval hold. The change of variable $y=x/L$ transfers this statement to $\mathbb T_L$ with normalized measure $dm_L=dx/L$ and coefficients $\widehat g(n)=\int g\overline{e_n}\,dm_L$.

[F4] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: integration of a continuous derivative on a compact interval gives the endpoint difference. Applied repeatedly to periodic smooth initial data, it gives rapid decay of their Fourier coefficients by integration by parts.

1.1 Define $j^\epsilon=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$. Adding the two equations in [F1] gives $\partial_t\rho^\epsilon+\partial_xj^\epsilon=0$. Subtracting them and multiplying by $c/\epsilon$ gives $\epsilon^2\partial_tj^\epsilon+2\lambda j^\epsilon=-c^2\partial_x\rho^\epsilon$. The initial condition implies $j^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=0$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Under [A1], take Fourier coefficients in $x$ in these two identities, with $\kappa_n$ and $\widehat{\cdot}(n)$ from [F1]; differentiate under the compact spatial integral using the smooth solution [F2], and integrate by parts in real and imaginary parts separately using [F4] after the measure-preserving rescaling $y=x/L$. Then $y_n^\epsilon(t):=\widehat{\rho^\epsilon(t)}(n)$ satisfies $\epsilon^2(y_n^\epsilon)''+2\lambda(y_n^\epsilon)'+c^2\kappa_n^2y_n^\epsilon=0$, $y_n^\epsilon(0)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)$, and $(y_n^\epsilon)'(0)=0$. The heat series in the Statement has coefficients $y_n(t)=\widehat{\rho_0}(n)e^{-D\kappa_n^2t}$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Repeated integration by parts in the real and imaginary parts using [F4] gives $\sum_n(1+|\kappa_n|)^r|\widehat{\rho_0}(n)|<\infty$ for every integer $r\ge0$; convergence follows by grouping $2^j\le|n|<2^{j+1}$ after choosing more than $r+1$ derivatives. Therefore the heat series and every differentiated series converge uniformly on compact time intervals, and its coefficient equation $y_n'=-D\kappa_n^2y_n$ proves $\partial_tu=D\partial_x^2u$ with $u(0)=\rho_0$. Any other smooth solution has the same scalar Fourier mode equations and initial coefficients, so [F3] proves uniqueness. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

**Given:** The domain, matrix fields, regularity, determinant and positivity conditions, and matrix equations in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-emg-fx-matrix-harmonic-problem]]: $\mathcal P_n$ consists of positive definite Hermitian complex $n\times n$ matrices with determinant one; $J=\Phi^{-1}d\Phi$ is differentiated entrywise and its Euclidean divergence is $\sum_a\partial_aJ_a$.

[F2] [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]: every Hermitian matrix on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues; positive matrices have positive square roots; and the finite trace is basis-independent and cyclic.

[F3] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]: for square matrices over a commutative field, $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.

[F4] [[thm-am-gm]]: for $n\ge1$ nonnegative reals $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{n-1}$, $\prod_j\lambda_j\le(\frac1n\sum_j\lambda_j)^n$, with equality exactly when all entries are equal.

[F5] [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: matrix products are computed by finite entry sums, and derivatives of their entries obey the ordinary product rule. [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies $\partial_a$ with differentiation along the $a$th coordinate line.

[F6] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: the closed bounded set $\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is compact, and every continuous real-valued function on it attains a maximum.



1.1 Put $u:=\operatorname{tr}\Psi$. The inverse formula in [F1] makes each $\Phi_i^{-1}$ smooth on $\overline\Omega$, so $u$ is smooth there. Differentiating $\Phi_i\Phi_i^{-1}=I_n$ entrywise and using the product rule gives $\partial_a\Phi_i^{-1}=-\Phi_i^{-1}(\partial_a\Phi_i)\Phi_i^{-1}=-J_{i,a}\Phi_i^{-1}$. Since $\partial_a\Phi_i=\Phi_iJ_{i,a}$, it follows that $\partial_a\Psi=\Phi_1\Delta J_a\Phi_0^{-1}$. The two divergence equations imply $\sum_a\partial_a\Delta J_a=0$. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

Let $\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_{n-1}>0$ be the eigenvalues of $\Phi_0$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis, determinant multiplicativity and $\det(U^\dagger U)=\det I_n=1$ for the unitary change-of-basis matrix $U$ give $\det\Phi_0=\prod_j\mu_j=1$; hence $\det(\Phi_0^{-1/2})=\prod_j\mu_j^{-1/2}=1$. For the positive eigenvalues $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{n-1}$ of $C$, orthonormal diagonalization gives $\det C=\prod_j\lambda_j$ and $\operatorname{tr}C=\sum_j\lambda_j$. [F11] If a differentiable real function has positive derivative throughout an interval, the mean-value theorem makes it strictly increasing there ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F12] A continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values ([[thm-intermediate-value]]).

[F13] A diffeomorphism is a bijective smooth map whose inverse is smooth ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]).

**Given:** The real periodic wave algorithm, $N\ge3$, $k>0$, and
$0<\lambda=k/h<1$.

[A1] The recurrence is extended complex-linearly to $\mathbb C^N$; its
real and imaginary parts separately satisfy the original real recurrence.

[F1] [[alg-gr-fx-periodic-wave-leapfrog]]: $D_h$ is the centered periodic
second difference, the startup is $u^1=u^0+kv^0+(k^2/2)D_hu^0$, and for
$n\ge1$ the update is $u^{n+1}=2u^n-u^{n-1}+k^2D_hu^n$.

[F2] [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]],
[[def-complex-exponential]]: $\mathbb C$ is a field with imaginary unit $i$,
$i^2=-1$, and the complex exponential is defined by its power series.

[F3] [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]:
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$, $\cos0=1$, and $\sin0=0$.

[F4] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]],
[[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: the double-angle
identity is $\cos(2x)-1=-2\sin^2x$.

[F5] [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]: sine and cosine
have period $2\pi$, the zero set of sine is $\pi\mathbb Z$, and for
$0<\ell<N$, $\sin(\pi\ell/N)\ne0$.

[F6] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: $|\sin x|\le1$
for every real $x$.

[F7] [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]: each nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative
square root.

[F8] [[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]: finite
cyclic shifts preserve the sum of an $N$-tuple.

[F9] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: shifts by $\pi$ negate
sine and cosine, and $\sin\pi=0$, $\cos\pi=-1$.



**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The period and zero-set facts in [F3, F5] make $e_\ell$ well-defined on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. Put $\theta_\ell=2\pi\ell/N$. By [F3] and [F4], $$ (D_he_\ell)(j)=h^{-2}\bigl(e^{i\theta_\ell}-2+e^{-i\theta_\ell}\bigr)e_\ell(j) =-4h^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)e_\ell(j). $$ Thus a mode sequence $u^n_j=a_ne_\ell(j)$ obeys $a_{n+1}-2c_\ell a_n+a_{n-1}=0$ for every update step. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 For the constant mode, define $\bar u^n=N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u_j^n$. By [F8], a cyclic shift preserves a finite sum, so $\sum_j(D_hu^n)_j=0$. Averaging the update [F1] therefore gives $\bar u^{n+1}=2\bar u^n-\bar u^{n-1}$, and averaging the startup gives $\bar u^1=\bar u^0+k\bar v^0$. Induction yields $\bar u^n=\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$; when $nk\le T$ its magnitude is at most $|\bar u^0|+T|\bar v^0|$, while nonzero $\bar v^0$ makes it unbounded as $n\to\infty$. [F1, F8, algebra]

1.3 For fixed $N$, list the $N-1$ numbers $2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$. Each is positive by [F5], since $\pi\ell/N$ is not an integer multiple of $\pi$. Taking the smaller of the first two positive numbers and then successively the smaller with each next number gives, by induction over this finite list, an attained positive minimum. The argument is for fixed $N$ only. [F5, algebra]

1.4 Suppose $N$ is even and $\lambda=1$. Repeated $\pi$-shift use of [F9] gives $\sin(\pi j)=0$ and $\cos(\pi j)=(-1)^j$ for every grid index $0\le j<N$; Euler's formula [F3] identifies the Fourier character $e_{N/2}(j)$ with the alternating array $(-1)^j$. 2.1 If $\ell\ne0$, [F5] and $0<\lambda<1$ imply $0<2\lambda^2\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)<2$, so $-1<c_\ell<1$. Then $r_\ell:=\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2}$ exists and is positive by [F7]. The sequence $Az_{\ell,+}^n+Bz_{\ell,-}^n$ obeys the recurrence in step 1.1 and has that initial pair; induction on $n$ therefore identifies it with $a_n$. Its absolute value is at most $|A|+|B|$ for all steps, so in particular on every finite slab. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $u_j^n=a_n(-1)^j$ and put $q_n:=(-1)^na_n$. The repeated-root recurrence from step 1.4 gives $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}=0$, so its first differences are constant and $q_n=a_0+n(-a_1-a_0)$. Einstein system would also need an error estimate for the initialization and
a discrete energy estimate for the actual reduced equations, including its
boundary treatment. The analytic finite-slab estimate on
[[thm-gr-fx-finite-slab-stability]] concerns continuum solutions of a fixed
gauge system and does not supply those discrete estimates.

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\geq1$, $0<\epsilon\leq1$, and the stated bounded-derivative symbol $a$.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Schwartz space and its finite-seminorm topology are defined in [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]].

[F2] The scaled Fourier transform is unitary on $L^2$ ([[lem-nrqmx-scaled-plancherel]]).

[F3] The normalized Gaussian Fourier integral is $\int e^{-|x|^2/(2\epsilon)}e^{-ip\cdot x/\epsilon}\,dx=(2\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}e^{-|p|^2/(2\epsilon)}$ ([[lem-euclidean-gaussian-fourier-transform-with-two-pi-normalization]]).

[F4] Tonelli's theorem applies to nonnegative product integrals ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F5] Absolutely integrable product integrals may be exchanged ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F6] $L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the first-variable-linear integral pairing is a complex Hilbert space ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

[F7] Every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space has a unique representing vector ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]).

[F8] Partial Fourier transformation of a Schwartz function in the $y$-variables is Schwartz jointly in the remaining $x$- and frequency variables; this follows by writing it as a full Fourier transform followed by inverse Fourier transform in $x$ ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]], [[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]]).


**Given:** The data of the Statement and [A1]–[F8]. Write $Z=(q,p)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $dZ=dq\,dp$.

1.1 For $Z=(q,p)$, define the normalized Gaussian packet $$ g_Z^\epsilon(x):=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{-|x-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}e^{ip\cdot(x-q/2)/\epsilon}. $$ Its norm is $1$ by [F3] at zero after the change of scale $x-q=\sqrt{\epsilon/2}\,s$. For $u\in\mathcal S$, put $V_\epsilon u(Z)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle$. The Fourier transform of the shifted Gaussian gives $$ \langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/4}e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}(2\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}\mathcal F_\epsilon\!\left(u(\,\cdot\,)e^{-|\cdot-q|^2/(2\epsilon)}\right)(p). $$ Plancherel [F2], followed by Tonelli [F4] and $\int e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dq=(\pi\epsilon)^{d/2}$, gives $$ \|V_\epsilon u\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int|\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle|^2\,dq\,dp=(\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int\!\!\int |u(x)|^2e^{-|x-q|^2/\epsilon}\,dx\,dq=\|u\|_2^2. $$ The middle equality follows from Plancherel [F2] for each fixed $q$; the final equality is the Gaussian integral [F3] in $q$, with Tonelli [F4]. The same identity holds for all $u\in L^2$ by [F2] and Tonelli [F4]. Polarization gives $\langle u,v\rangle=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle\overline{\langle v,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle}\,dZ$, hence the weak resolution $$ u=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}\langle u,g_Z^\epsilon\rangle g_Z^\epsilon\,dZ . $$ [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

If $|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon$, its $L^1$ norm is $1$, hence $|B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq\|a\|_\infty$. If $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$, then $$ L_\delta:=\frac{\epsilon}{i|\delta|^2}\nabla_w\phi_\delta\cdot\nabla_w,\qquad \phi_\delta(w):=-\sigma(w,\delta) $$ satisfies $L_\delta e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}=e^{i\phi_\delta(w)/\epsilon}$, since $|\nabla_w\phi_\delta|=|\delta|$. Integrating by parts $N_d$ times against the Gaussian, and scaling $w=\sqrt\epsilon\,s$, shows that every derivative on the Gaussian contributes a factor bounded by $\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$; a derivative on $a$ contributes $\epsilon/|\delta|\leq\sqrt\epsilon/|\delta|$, since $|\delta|>\sqrt\epsilon$ and $\epsilon\leq1$. Thus $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'},g_Z)|\leq C_d\left(\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\epsilon^{|\alpha|/2}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty\right)(1+|\delta|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}\leq C_dD(a)(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}, $$ where $D(a)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq N_d}\|\partial^\alpha a\|_\infty$. Its partial Fourier transform in $x$ is Schwartz in $(p,q)$ by the same full Fourier/inverse Fourier argument as [F8]. The additional phase $e^{ip\cdot q/(2\epsilon)}$ in $\langle u,g_{q,p}^\epsilon\rangle$ has derivatives that are polynomial factors, so the packet coefficient $V_\epsilon u$ remains Schwartz in $Z=(q,p)$. The Schwartz seminorms of $Z\mapsto g_Z^\epsilon$ grow at most polynomially in $Z$, so the resolution integral in step 1.1 converges in every Schwartz seminorm. The product $u(x+y/2)\overline{v(x-y/2)}$ is Schwartz in $(x,y)$; its partial Fourier transform is Schwartz by [F8], so $\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\in\mathcal S$ and $|B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\le\|a\|_\infty\|\mathcal W_\epsilon[u,v]\|_1$ proves continuity of the form in Schwartz seminorms. If $a\in\mathcal S$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz; the kernel pairing is absolutely convergent, and the change $q=(x+y)/2,\ r=x-y$, followed by $r\mapsto-y$, identifies it with $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)$. Thus the bounded-symbol form extends the kernel definition on Schwartz symbols. Applying the continuous form to the two Schwartz-convergent resolutions is valid; Fubini [F5] for the resulting absolutely integrable products gives $$ B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\iint B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon)V_\epsilon u(Z')\overline{V_\epsilon v(Z)}\,dZ'\,dZ . $$ [step 1.1, F1, F5, F8, algebra]

3.1 Partition $\mathbb R^{2d}$ into cubes of side $\sqrt\epsilon$. For each fixed $Z$, the sum of $(1+|Z-Z'|/\sqrt\epsilon)^{-N_d}$ over these cubes, each weighted by its volume $\epsilon^d$, is at most $C_d\epsilon^d\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^{2d}}(1+|k|)^{-N_d}\leq C_d'\epsilon^d$, since $N_d=4d+4>2d$. The same holds with $Z,Z'$ interchanged. Thus the integral kernel $$ K_\epsilon(Z,Z'):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}B_{\epsilon,a}(g_{Z'}^\epsilon,g_Z^\epsilon) $$ has uniformly bounded row and column $L^1$ norms, each at most $C_dD(a)$. Integrating in $Z$ and using the column bound yields $\|K_\epsilon f\|_2\leq C_dD(a)\|f\|_2$. Applying this estimate to step 2.1 and using the isometry in step 1.1 proves $$ |B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)|\leq C_dD(a)\|V_\epsilon u\|_2\|V_\epsilon v\|_2=C_dD(a)\|u\|_2\|v\|_2 . $$ [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, A1, F4, algebra]

4.1 For fixed $u\in\mathcal S$, the bounded form in step 3.1 extends continuously in $v$ to $L^2$, which is a Hilbert space by [F6], and $v\mapsto\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}$ is a bounded linear functional there. Riesz representation [F7] gives a unique $y\in L^2$ with $\overline{B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)}=\langle v,y\rangle$ for every $v\in L^2$; conjugate symmetry gives $B_{\epsilon,a}(u,v)=\langle y,v\rangle$, so set $A_\epsilon u=y$. Its norm is at most $C_dD(a)\|u\|_2$. Uniqueness makes $u\mapsto A_\epsilon u$ linear on $\mathcal S$, and this bound extends it uniquely to $L^2$. Hence the operator norm is at most $C_dD(a)$. [given, A1, step 3.1, F6, F7, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $d,m\ge1$, a spanning family $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$, its synthesis map $S$, Gram matrix $G=S^*S$, Moore–Penrose inverse $G^+$, and canonical dual $D_a$.

[A1] The finite family $F_1,\ldots,F_m$ spans $\mathsf H_d$ over $\mathbb R$, as required in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-nrqmx-finite-hermitian-frame-and-gram-pseudoinverse]]: $\mathsf H_d$ is a real space with the trace pairing $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$; $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; $D_a=\sum_b(G^+)_{ba}F_b$.

[F2] [[lem-nrqmx-finite-hermitian-trace-inner-product]]: the Hilbert–Schmidt trace pairing is a real inner product, $G=S^*S$ is real positive semidefinite, and $\ker G=\ker S$.

[F3] [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]: every finite Hermitian matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

[F4] [[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]]: $G^+$ satisfies $GG^+G=G$, $G^+GG^+=G^+$, and both $GG^+$ and $G^+G$ are self-adjoint.

[F5] [[thm-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse-exists-and-is-unique]]: every finite real matrix has a unique matrix satisfying the four Penrose equations.



1.1 By [F2], $G$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite, $G=S^*S$, and $\ker G=\ker S$. The coordinate formula for the adjoint is $(S^*X)_a=\langle F_a,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)$ by [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Regard the real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $G$ as a complex Hermitian matrix and apply [F3]. Its eigenvalues are real. If $z=x+iy$ is in the complex eigenspace for a real eigenvalue $\lambda$, then realness of $G$ gives $Gx=\lambda x$ and $Gy=\lambda y$; thus that eigenspace is the complexification of its real eigenspace. Real eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, since $Gu=\lambda u$, $Gv=\mu v$, and symmetry give $(\lambda-\mu)u^{\mathsf T}v=0$. Their real direct sum is $\mathbb R^m$ because the complex eigenspaces span $\mathbb C^m$ by [F3] and each is the complexification of its real eigenspace. Choosing a real orthonormal basis in each gives a real spectral resolution $G=\sum_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda P_\lambda$ with real orthogonal projections whose sum is $I$. Put $H_0=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Orthogonality gives $GH_0G=G$, $H_0GH_0=H_0$, and $GH_0=H_0G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda$, which are self-adjoint. Thus $H_0$ satisfies the four Penrose equations [F4], and uniqueness in [F5] gives $H_0=G^+$. Consequently $Q=G^+G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda$ is an orthogonal projection and $\ker Q=\ker G$, so $\operatorname{Ran}(I-Q)=\ker G=\ker S$ by [F2]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The synthesis map of the canonical dual is $D=SG^+$ by [F1]. For any $X\in\mathsf H_d$, the spanning hypothesis [A1] supplies $c\in\mathbb R^m$ with $X=Sc$. Then $$ D(S^*X)=SG^+S^*Sc=SG^+Gc=SQc=Sc=X, $$ because $c-Qc\in\operatorname{Ran}(I-Q)=\ker S$ by step 2.1. The coordinates of $S^*X$ are $\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)$ by step 1.1, which proves the stated sum. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Apply this to $W=e^{\lambda S}$ and then step 1.1 to get $\mathbb P(f-p\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda nt+n\lambda^2/8}$. Setting $\lambda=4t$ gives $e^{-2nt^2}$. [given, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

**Given:** The six displayed matrices and a density matrix $\rho$ on $\mathbb C^2$.

[A1] The Pauli matrices and effects are the finite matrices and operators in the Example.

[A2] $\rho$ is Hermitian, positive semidefinite, and has trace one.

[F1] [[thm-nrqmx-tomography-identifiability-stability]]: for a spanning finite POVM, exact probabilities reconstruct $\rho$, and the linear-inversion output is $\sum_af_aD_a$ for its canonical dual.

[F2] [[lem-nrqmx-frame-pseudoinverse-reconstruction]]: for a positive semidefinite Gram matrix with spectral projections $P_\lambda$ at positive eigenvalues, $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$.

[F3] [[def-nrqmx-finite-hermitian-frame-and-gram-pseudoinverse]]: $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$ and $D_a=\sum_b(G^+)_{ba}F_b$.



1.1 Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$; reversing the order negates each mixed product. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$. Since a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathsf H_2=4$; the four nonzero orthogonal matrices $I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ form a basis. Every trace-one Hermitian $\rho$ therefore has the stated form with $r_j=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\in\mathbb R$. Positivity [A2] restricts $|r|\le1$, since $(r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z)^2=|r|^2I$ and the eigenvalues of $\rho$ are $(1\pm|r|)/2$. [A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $1,-1$ by step 1.1, so $F_{j,\pm}$ has eigenvalues $1/3,0$ and is positive. For each $j$, $F_{j,+}+F_{j,-}=I/3$; summing over $x,y,z$ gives $I$. Also $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, so each $\sigma_j$ lies in the real span of the effects. Since $I$ is their sum, the basis in step 1.1 shows that the effects span $\mathsf H_2$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In the coordinate order $(x+,x-,y+,y-,z+,z-)$, direct multiplication and step 1.1 give $G_{(j,s),(k,t)}=\frac1{36}\operatorname{Tr}((I+s\sigma_j)(I+t\sigma_k))=\frac1{18}(1+st\,\delta_{jk})$ for $s,t\in\{+1,-1\}$. Thus the diagonal entries are $1/9$, opposite outcomes on one axis have entry $0$, and distinct axes have entry $1/18$. Let $u=(1,1,1,1,1,1)$ and $v_j=e_{j+}-e_{j-}$. Then $Gu=u/3$, $Gv_j=v_j/9$, and $G$ vanishes on vectors $(s_x,s_x,s_y,s_y,s_z,s_z)$ with $s_x+s_y+s_z=0$. These mutually orthogonal subspaces have dimensions $1,3,2$ and span $\mathbb R^6$. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2] and the eigenspaces in step 3.1, $G^+=3P_u+9\sum_jP_{v_j}$, where $P_u=uu^\mathsf T/6$ and $P_{v_j}=v_jv_j^\mathsf T/2$. The $e_{j+}$ column of $G^+$ is $u/2+9v_j/2$. Applying the canonical-dual formula [F3], using $\sum_{k,\pm}F_{k,\pm}=I$ and $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, gives $D_{j,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_j$; similarly $D_{j,-}=\frac12I-\frac32\sigma_j$. The probabilities are $p_{j,\pm}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_{j,\pm})=(1\pm r_j)/6$, so $\sum_{j,\pm}p_{j,\pm}D_{j,\pm}=\frac12I+\frac12\sum_jr_j\sigma_j=\rho$, in agreement with [F1]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The frequency vector with $f_{x,+}=1$ and all other entries zero is nonnegative and sums to one. Its output is $D_{x,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_x$, whose eigenvalues are $2$ and $-1$. It is Hermitian but not positive, so the linear-inversion procedure does not preserve positivity for every frequency vector. [A1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, and $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The Weyl operator on Schwartz functions has the integral kernel formula in [[def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner]].

[F2] The scaled Fourier transform is unitary on $L^2$, so its inverse preserves $L^2$ norms ([[lem-nrqmx-scaled-plancherel]]).

[F3] Tonelli's theorem permits the iterated integrals of the nonnegative function $|K_\epsilon|^2$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F4] $L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, with $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u\overline v$ linear in its first argument, is a complex Hilbert space ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).


**Given:** The data and Fourier convention of the Statement and [A1], [F1]–[F4].

1.1 Set $q=(x+y)/2$ and $r=x-y$. Then $x=q+r/2$, $y=q-r/2$, and the absolute Jacobian of $(q,r)\mapsto(x,y)$ is $1$. In these coordinates, $$ K_\epsilon(q,r)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{ir\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a(q,\xi)\,d\xi=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}(\mathcal F_\epsilon^{-1}a(q,\cdot))(r). $$ Applying [F2] to the $\xi$-section for each $q$, then [F3] to integrate the resulting nonnegative function in $q$, gives $$ \|K_\epsilon\|_2^2=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|a(q,\xi)|^2\,d\xi\,dq=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\|a\|_2^2. $$ Thus $K_\epsilon\in L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$ with the asserted norm. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, the section $K_\epsilon(x,\cdot)$ lies in $L^2$ for almost every $x$ by [F3]. For those $x$, define $(A_\epsilon u)(x)=\int K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the Hilbert space pairing [F4] gives $$ |A_\epsilon u(x)|^2\leq\left(\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)|^2\,dy\right)\|u\|_2^2. $$ Integrating in $x$ and using [F3] shows $A_\epsilon u\in L^2$ and $\|A_\epsilon u\|_2\leq\|K_\epsilon\|_2\|u\|_2$. For $u\in\mathcal S$, the kernel formula defining $A_\epsilon u$ is exactly [F1], so this is the required bounded extension. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The selected first-variation decomposition, a smooth vector field
$\xi$, its local action on the fields, and diffeomorphism covariance of
$\mathcal L$.

[A1] $\delta_\xi\phi=\mathcal L_\xi\phi$ and
$\delta_\xi\mathcal L=\mathcal L_\xi\mathcal L$.

[F1] The first-variation decomposition is
$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$.
[[def-gr-fx-covariant-presymplectic-current]]

[F2] Cartan's identity is
$\mathcal L_\xi\alpha=d_M(\iota_\xi\alpha)+\iota_\xi(d_M\alpha)$ for every
differential form $\alpha$. [[thm-cartans-magic-formula]]

[F3] A closed smooth $k$-form on a star-shaped coordinate domain has a
primitive for each $1\le k\le4$.
[[lem-gr-fx-star-shaped-poincare-homotopy]]

[F4] For a tensor field and the local flow $\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,
$\mathcal L_\xi T=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_0\Phi_t^*T$.
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]]



**Given:** As in [A1] and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 By [F4], $\mathcal L_\xi\mathcal L$ is the derivative of the pullback of $\mathcal L$ along the local flow. Since $\mathcal L$ is a four-form on a four-manifold, $d_M\mathcal L=0$ by degree. Cartan's identity [F2] gives $\delta_\xi\mathcal L=\mathcal L_\xi\mathcal L =d_M(\iota_\xi\mathcal L)$. [A1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F1] to the variation $\delta_\xi\phi=\mathcal L_\xi\phi$ and equate it with step 1.1: $E_\phi[\mathcal L_\xi\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\phi) =d_M(\iota_\xi\mathcal L)$. Rearranging gives $d_MJ_\xi=-E_\phi[\mathcal L_\xi\phi]$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $E_\phi=0$, step 2.1 gives $d_MJ_\xi=0$. Restrict to any star-shaped coordinate neighborhood and apply [F3] with $k=3$; this yields a two-form $Q_\xi$ on that neighborhood such that $J_\xi=d_MQ_\xi$ there. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

without a separate cohomological argument. It asserts a classical identity
only; it constructs no measure, Hilbert space, or anomaly-free quantization.

**Given:** A fixed plane $z$, the stated smooth $L^2$ scalar field $u_z$ with
nonzero $L^2$ class and the stated integer-winding form.

[F1] The paraxial scalar field and its SI field interpretation are those of the
angular-spectrum Definition. [[def-emx-angular-spectrum]] [[def-em-si-conventions]]

[F2] The real partial derivatives are those on the fixed laboratory spatial
slice, and complex exponentiation satisfies $\exp'=\exp$. [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]

[F3] The field uses the complex exponential and conjugation/modulus operations
defined on all complex numbers. [[def-complex-exponential]] [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]



1.1 For $r>0$, the angular vector field $-y\partial_x+x\partial_y$ is $\partial_\phi$ in polar coordinates. By the chain rule and [F2]–[F3], $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=-i\partial_\phi(fe^{i\ell\phi}) =\ell fe^{i\ell\phi}=\ell u_z$. The required axis form makes $u_z$ smooth at the origin: for $\ell\ge0$ its angular factor is $(x+iy)^\ell$, and for $\ell<0$ it is $(x-iy)^{|\ell|}$, each multiplied by the smooth radial factor $g(x^2+y^2)$. The rotation vector field vanishes at the origin, so the same identity holds there as well. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Step 1.1 gives $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z=\ell u_z$ everywhere, hence $L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z\in L^2$ because $u_z\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Therefore $\langle L_z^{\mathrm{sc}}u_z,u_z\rangle_2 =\int_{\mathbb R^2}\ell|u_z|^2\,d^2x =\ell\langle u_z,u_z\rangle_2$; the denominator is positive since $u_z$ is nonzero. Division proves the claimed identity. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎



The axis hypothesis is stated as a smooth extension condition; the bound
$f(r)=O(r^{|\ell|})$ alone would not guarantee smoothness. No radial
integration by parts is used. The scalar generator is dimensionless and does
not by itself determine a torque or a photon angular momentum.

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\geq1$, $0<\epsilon\leq1$, and $a,b\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$.

[A1] Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] Weyl quantization uses the kernel and Fourier conventions of [[def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner]].

[F2] The square-integrable kernel estimate extends each Schwartz Weyl operator boundedly to $L^2$ ([[lem-nrqmx-weyl-hilbert-schmidt-bound]]).

[F3] The Fourier transform maps Schwartz space continuously to itself ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]).

[F4] Fourier inversion on Schwartz space is pointwise and absolutely convergent ([[thm-fourier-inversion-on-schwartz-space]]).

[F5] Fubini's theorem applies to absolutely integrable products on Euclidean product spaces ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

[F6] Translations $x\mapsto x+\epsilon p$ preserve Lebesgue integrals by the $C^1$ change-of-variables theorem ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

[F7] Schwartz functions are dense in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]).


**Given:** The data of the Statement and [A1]–[F7]. For $z=(x,\xi)$ and $\lambda=(q,p)$, write $\lambda\cdot z=q\cdot x+p\cdot\xi$ and $\sigma(\lambda,\mu)=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$ for $\mu=(q',p')$.

1.1 Let $\widehat a(\lambda)=\int e^{-i\lambda\cdot z}a(z)\,dz$, and similarly for $b$. These are rescaled versions of the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform; [F3] and [F4] imply they are Schwartz, integrable, and have inverse $a(z)=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int e^{i\lambda\cdot z}\widehat a(\lambda)\,d\lambda$. For $\lambda=(q,p)$, define the unitary map $$ (T^\epsilon_{q,p}u)(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p). $$ The phase has modulus one and [F6] preserves the norm under translation, so $T^\epsilon_{q,p}$ is unitary, with inverse given by reversing the translation and phase. Fourier inversion [F4], this formula, Fubini [F5] and the translation change of variables [F6] give the scalar form representation $$ \mathcal B_a(u,v):=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle T^\epsilon_\lambda u,v\rangle\,d\lambda . $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, this scalar integral is absolutely convergent and bounded by $(2\pi)^{-2d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$. For Schwartz $u,v$, use $T^\epsilon_{q,p}u(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p)$, set $y=x+\epsilon p$, and then apply Fourier inversion in $q$: $\int e^{iq\cdot(x+y)/2}\widehat a(q,(y-x)/\epsilon)\,dq=(2\pi)^d\int e^{-i(y-x)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a((x+y)/2,\xi)\,d\xi$. This gives $\mathcal B_a(u,v)=\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,v\rangle$. Both forms are bounded on $L^2\times L^2$, so [F7] extends their equality from the dense Schwartz subspace to all $L^2$ pairs; [F2] supplies the bounded Weyl extension. Since $T_\lambda^\epsilon$ is unitary, $\langle T_\mu^\epsilon u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle=\langle T_\lambda^\epsilon T_\mu^\epsilon u,v\rangle$; the double integral is absolutely convergent with majorant $(2\pi)^{-4d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|\widehat b\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, so Fubini and the Weyl relation give $$ c_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,d\lambda\,d\mu . $$ The phase-space Fourier coefficient of $\{a,b\}$ is $-\sigma(\lambda,\mu)\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)$; this follows by differentiating the Fourier modes in the explicitly fixed Poisson convention. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $$ e^{-i\epsilon\sigma/2}=1-\frac{i\epsilon\sigma}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^2\sigma^2}{4}\int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}\,ds. $$ Set $$ R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu):=\frac{\sigma(\lambda,\mu)^2}{4} \int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,ds . $$ Consequently the symbol remainder is $$ r_\epsilon(z)=-(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)\,d\lambda\,d\mu. $$ For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ with $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le K:=4d+4$, differentiate $|\alpha|$ times in $z$ and integrate by parts $|\beta|$ times in $\lambda$ to estimate $z^\beta\partial_z^\alpha r_\epsilon(z)$. This proves $p_K(r_\epsilon)\le C_dp_M(a)p_M(b)$, uniformly in $\epsilon$. The same argument with any fixed larger $K$ proves every Schwartz seminorm of $r_\epsilon$ is finite, so $r_\epsilon\in\mathcal S$. Hence $c_\epsilon=ab+\frac{i\epsilon}{2}\{a,b\}+\epsilon^2r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz, and the weak Fourier representation from step 1.1 identifies the product in step 2.1 with $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(c_\epsilon)$. 4.1 The kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)$, in $q=(x+y)/2$, $s=x-y$, is $$ K_\epsilon(q,s)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{is\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_\epsilon(q,\xi)\,d\xi. $$ Since $K=4d+4\ge2d+2$, $\langle(q,\xi)\rangle^K\ge\langle q\rangle^{d+1}\langle\xi\rangle^{d+1}$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\langle\xi\rangle^{-d-1}d\xi<\infty$ imply $\int|\partial_\xi^\gamma r_\epsilon(q,\xi)|\,d\xi\le C_dp_K(r_\epsilon)\langle q\rangle^{-d-1}$ for $|\gamma|\le2d+2$. Combining steps 2.1–3.1 proves the asserted Weyl composition formula with the plus sign fixed by $[Q_j,P_k]=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}$. [step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The finite-dimensional Hilbert space, finite projection-valued measures, and joint POVM defined in the Statement.

[A1] The families $(P_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Q_j)_{j\in J}$ each consist of pairwise orthogonal projections summing to $I_H$.

[F1] [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]]: a finite POVM is a family of effects $0\le F_a\le I$ summing to $I$; its marginals are finite POVMs.

[F2] [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]]: a finite positive semidefinite matrix has a positive square root defined by its spectral resolution.



1.1 Suppose all $P_i$ commute with all $Q_j$. Then $G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$ is self-adjoint, since $(P_iQ_j)^*=Q_jP_i=P_iQ_j$, and is idempotent, since $(P_iQ_j)^2=P_i^2Q_j^2=P_iQ_j$. For any $x$, $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\langle G_{ij}x,G_{ij}x\rangle\ge0$, so each is positive; the sum identity makes each bounded above by $I_H$. Finite summation gives $\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}=(\sum_iP_i)(\sum_jQ_j)=I_H$, and the two marginal sums are $P_i$ and $Q_j$. So this family is a joint POVM. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Conversely, suppose a joint POVM $(G_{ij})$ exists. For each pair, $0\le G_{ij}\le P_i$ because $P_i-G_{ij}=\sum_{k\ne j}G_{ik}\ge0$, and similarly $0\le G_{ij}\le Q_j$. If $x\in\ker P_i$, then $0\le\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle\le\langle P_ix,x\rangle=0$. By [F2], $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\|G_{ij}^{1/2}x\|^2$, hence $G_{ij}x=0$ and $G_{ij}(I-P_i)=0$. Taking adjoints gives $(I-P_i)G_{ij}=0$, so $G_{ij}=P_iG_{ij}P_i$. The same argument yields $G_{ij}=Q_jG_{ij}Q_j$. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Using $P_i=\sum_kG_{ik}$ and $Q_j=\sum_\ell G_{\ell j}$, we obtain $P_iQ_j=\sum_kG_{ik}Q_j$. The support relation $G_{ik}=Q_kG_{ik}Q_k$ from step 1.2 makes every term with $k\ne j$ zero, and the $k=j$ term is $G_{ij}$. Therefore $P_iQ_j=G_{ij}$. Since $G_{ij}$ is self-adjoint, taking adjoints gives $Q_jP_i=G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$. This proves commutation and uniqueness. [A1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎



The sharp projection hypothesis is essential. General POVMs can be jointly measurable even when their effects do not commute; no commutation criterion for arbitrary POVMs is asserted here.
